outro.title: AI Fluency **Insights**
outro.sub: See how you work with Claude Code. Get a little better every week.

beats.say: This is AI Fluency Insights. A private dashboard that shows how you actually work with Claude Code.
Claude Code is powerful, but how well you use it is invisible. Two developers can have the same tool, and get completely different results. And nothing tells either of them which one they are.

Claude Code does give you a few ways to look at usage. Usage, context, status, insights, a status line. But each one answers a single narrow question, for a single session, and most of it disappears when you clear the conversation.
So the simple questions go unanswered. How much did I use last month? Is Claude's code actually getting tested? Am I better at this than I was a month ago? And what should I do differently?

AI Fluency Insights answers those. It reads the log files Claude Code already saves on your machine, does the maths locally, and turns them into one dashboard. It never calls an A P I, it costs zero tokens, and nothing ever leaves your computer.
beats.cap: It reads the log files Claude Code already saves on your machine, does the maths locally, and turns them into one dashboard. It never calls an API, costs zero tokens, and nothing leaves your computer.

beats.say: {DATA} Let's take a tour, tab by tab.
We start on the Overview. At the top is your momentum: a day streak, your best streak, and how many days you have used Claude Code in total.
Next, plan usage limits. With the optional status line hook installed, this shows your real five hour and weekly limits straight from Anthropic, not a guess.
Then the headline numbers. Input and output tokens, how much came from cache, and the estimated A P I cost. On a subscription that is the value you received, not a bill.
beats.cap: Then the headline numbers. Input and output tokens, how much came from cache, and the estimated API cost. On a subscription, that is the value you received, not a bill.

beats.say: Lines of code Claude actually wrote, your prompts, your sessions, and friction: the times you interrupted Claude, or a tool call failed.
Every card also shows how it moved, compared with the previous period of the same length.
My favourite is leverage. It is Claude's output divided by what you typed. Fifty times means every token you type gets fifty back.
The range buttons control the whole page. Seven days, thirty, ninety, or all time, or pick custom dates.
Below, daily tokens. Cache reads dominate, and that is good: it means Claude re-used context instead of reprocessing it, which keeps long sessions cheap.
You versus Claude. Tokens you typed against tokens Claude produced, on a log scale. The gap between the two lines is your leverage, drawn out.
Lines of code per day, and exploration versus building. Reading is exploration, editing is building. Neither is better. What matters is that the mix matches what you meant to do that day.
Time and Focus is the sustainability tab. Active time is counted in ten minute buckets of real activity, so it is much closer to hands-on time than raw session length.
It shows your longest focus block, and how much of your work happened late at night or at weekends. This is something to reflect on, not a number to maximise.
The heatmap shows your working rhythm, by weekday and hour. It is the quickest way to spot a late night habit.
Task mix sorts each session into feature, bug fix, refactor, docs or exploration, using Claude's own session titles. And friction per day points you at the painful sessions.
Tools and Models shows which models do the heavy lifting, and where the estimated cost comes from.
Autonomy mode shows how much you let Claude act without asking, and Delegation shows the subagents you spawned, by type.
Tool usage and slash commands give you a quick portrait of how you and Claude actually work together.
Projects breaks everything down per project: tokens, lines of code, prompts, sessions and cost. Click any row for a deep dive.
Here is one project on its own: a daily chart, its sessions with their titles, and the files Claude edited most.
Git branches attribute output to each branch, and most edited files show where Claude's code actually landed.
And the longest prompts. Fun, and sometimes revealing about what you over-explain.
Weekly Report is built for one job: your standup writes itself. Browse any week with previous and next.
Claude Code already stores a title for every session. They are grouped here by project, with date, duration and lines of code: ready made standup bullets.
The AI Fluency report scores four skills from zero to a hundred, adapted from Anthropic's A I fluency framework. Orange is this week. Blue is last week.
beats.cap: The AI Fluency report scores four skills from 0 to 100, adapted from Anthropic's AI fluency framework. Orange is this week. Blue is last week.

beats.say: Delegation: do you hand Claude real work? Description: do your prompts land first time? Discernment: do you review and steer? Diligence: do you verify what was written?
Each week the data also picks one reflection question worth sitting with. A good one to take into your next one to one.
And copy as markdown turns the whole week into a formatted update for Slack or Teams, in one click.
My Adoption is a personal scorecard. A score from zero to a hundred, and one of six levels, from Explorer up to Pro Max.
Four pillars sit behind it. Habit: do you show up regularly? Range: do you use what Claude Code offers? Craft: do you work with it well? Impact: what does it get done for you?
What changed lately, and your adoption journey. Started, recurring, integrated, and verified outcomes, each backed by evidence from your own logs.
Your next three moves are picked from your own data, with a one line how to. It is rule based. No AI, and no tokens.
A habit calendar, and a checklist of ten features: the ones you use, and how to start the ones you do not.
It only ever compares you with your own past. It is for you, not for a manager.
Now the Engineering insight tabs. Flow asks how smoothly work moves. Turn time, and clean first pass turns: no error, no interruption, no correction.
Failures that got fixed, versus stuck loops of three or more in a row. And where tool time goes, so you can see which commands eat the clock.
Quality asks whether speed comes with checking. How often a test, build or lint ran after Claude's last edit, and whether the first run passed.
Rework hotspots show files edited again and again, and safety signals flag things like force pushes or recursive deletes.
Value is what it costs, and what you get back. Cost per hundred lines, cost per verified session, and how much caching saved you.
Daily cost with the spikes marked, so you can find what caused them. There is no score here, because dollars have no universal good. Each figure is compared with your previous period.
Advisor turns all of that into your top moves. Each one quotes its own evidence, and you can start it as an experiment, then watch the number move.
It balances the list with what is going well, because a coach that only criticises does not get used.
Data Health is the honesty tab. It shows what your logs can and cannot measure, so a missing signal shows up as missing, never as zero.

do.spot: card:What your logs let us measure

beats.say: Every number in the dashboard carries a badge: Observed, Derived, Proxy or Estimated. So a rough signal is never presented as a fact.
The metric catalog lists the formula and the limitation for every metric. And privacy mode hides titles, prompts and file names on screen.
That is AI Fluency Insights. One Python file, standard library only, no accounts and no tokens. Run it, open local host eight seven eight seven, and see how you work with Claude Code.
beats.cap: That is AI Fluency Insights. One Python file, standard library only, no accounts, no tokens. Run it, open localhost:8787, and see how you work with Claude Code.

beats.say: And get a little better at it, every week.
